title: Linear & Polynomial Regression
html:
Linear regression predicts a number as a weighted sum of the features. It is fast, interpretable, the baseline for every regression problem — and, with polynomial features, it can fit curves too.

ŷ = w₀ + w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + … + wₚxₚ

Ordinary least squares

OLS chooses the weights that minimise the sum of squared residuals Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)². The minimiser has a closed form, the normal equation (in practice solved with a stable least-squares routine rather than an explicit inverse):

w = (XᵀX)⁻¹ Xᵀ y (X includes a column of 1s for the intercept)

Reading the coefficients

wⱼ is the expected change in ŷ when xⱼ increases by one unit with the other features held fixed. Two cautions: coefficients depend on the feature's units (standardise features to compare magnitudes), and they describe association in this data, not cause and effect.

Assumptions (and what breaks when they fail)

AssumptionCheckIf violated
Linearity — E[y | x] is linear in the parametersResiduals vs fitted values show no patternBiased predictions → transform features, add polynomial terms, or use a non-linear model
Independent errorsNo autocorrelation in residuals over time/order (Durbin-Watson)Standard errors too small → time-series models, clustered errors
Homoscedasticity — constant error varianceNo funnel shape in residuals vs fittedUnreliable intervals/p-values → log-transform y, weighted least squares, robust standard errors
Normal errorsQ–Q plot of residualsOnly affects small-sample confidence intervals and p-values — not the predictions
No perfect multicollinearityVariance inflation factor (VIF) — above ~5–10 is a warningUnstable, uninterpretable coefficients → drop/combine features, Ridge
Key point

Under linearity, exogeneity (E[ε | X] = 0) and uncorrelated constant-variance errors, OLS is the best linear unbiased estimator (Gauss–Markov). Normality is not required for that — only for exact small-sample tests. For p-values and confidence intervals use statsmodels' OLS; scikit-learn focuses on prediction.

Multicollinearity check — x3 is almost x1 + x2, so each of them is well predicted by the others:

Polynomial regression

Add powers (and products) of the features, then fit an ordinary linear model. The model is still linear in its parameters, so OLS applies unchanged. Choose the degree with cross-validation — too high overfits:

Watch out

With several features, PolynomialFeatures(degree=d) creates every product up to degree d — the column count explodes (10 features, degree 3 → 286 columns). Combine it with scaling and Ridge, or use splines (SplineTransformer) or a tree model.

Do

Use as a fast, interpretable baseline; when relationships are roughly linear; when you need coefficients to explain.

Avoid

Expect it to capture interactions or thresholds you didn't engineer; trust coefficients of correlated features; extrapolate far beyond the training range.

What is the difference between R² and adjusted R²?

R² never decreases when you add a feature, even a useless one. Adjusted R² = 1 − (1 − R²)(n − 1)/(n − p − 1) penalises the number of predictors p, so it only rises if a new feature helps more than chance would.

Why not use linear regression for classification?

Its outputs aren't bounded to [0, 1], so they aren't probabilities, and squared error on 0/1 labels lets far-away, correctly classified points drag the boundary. Logistic regression models the log-odds instead and is fitted by maximum likelihood.

What does multicollinearity do to a linear regression?

Predictions can remain fine, but coefficients become unstable (large standard errors, signs that flip with small data changes) because the model can't tell the correlated features' effects apart. Detect with VIF; fix by dropping or combining features, or with Ridge regularisation.
